en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
Pāṭhavagga 22.
The Training Rule on Fewer Than Five Repairs.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Monastery.
Now at that time, a certain potter had invited the monks,
saying, "Venerable sirs, for whichever of you need a bowl,
I [shall provide] a bowl. At that time, however, the monks did not know moderation and requested many bowls.
Those who had small bowls requested large ones;
those who had large bowls requested small ones.
Consequently, as that potter was making many bowls for the monks, he was unable to produce other merchandise for sale.
He could not even support himself; his wife and children were exhausted.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, fail to know moderation and request so many bowls?”
"This man, making so many bowls, is unable to produce any other merchandise for sale;
he cannot even support himself, and his wife and children are suffering," they said.
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing him.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can these monks, lacking moderation, request many bowls?
Then those monks, having rebuked them in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before].
“Is it true, monks, that the monks do not know moderation and ask for many bowls?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
“How, monks, could those foolish men, not knowing moderation, request many bowls?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“Monks, one should not request an almsbowl. Whoever should request one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, a certain monk’s almsbowl was broken.
Then that monk, being anxious because “the Blessed One has prohibited requesting an almsbowl,” did not request one.
He wandered for alms with his hands [extended].
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can these ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, wander for alms with their hands [extended], just like the followers of other sects?”
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, to request a bowl when a bowl is lost or broken.
Now at that time, the group of six monks, thinking,
“It has been permitted by the Blessed One to request a bowl when a bowl is lost or broken,” [requested bowls] even for a slight break or a slight crack.
Even by merely scratching [the clay], they would request many bowls.
Consequently, while that potter was making so many bowls for the monks, he was unable to produce other merchandise for sale;
he could not even support himself, and his wife and children suffered.
People likewise complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, not knowing moderation, request so many bowls?
This man, while making so many bowls for them, cannot produce other merchandise for sale; he does not even support himself, and his wife and children are suffering.”
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can the group-of-six monks request many bowls when even a small one is broken, even a small one is cracked, or even when it is merely scratched?"
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, monks, that you ask for many bowls even for a mere trifle that is broken, a mere trifle that is cracked, or even merely scratched?
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, request many bowls even for a mere slight break, a mere slight crack, or even a mere scratch?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whatever monk, with an alms-bowl having fewer than five mends, should have another new bowl made, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
That bowl must be relinquished by that monk to an assembly of monks.”
And whoever is the last bowl in that assembly of monks, that should be given to that monk with the words: “Monk, this bowl is to be kept by you until it breaks.
This is the proper procedure in this matter.
“But whoever... refers to...
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
A bowl called "having fewer than five bands" is one that has no band,
or one band, or two bands, or three bands, or four bands.
A bowl called "without a band-position" is a bowl...
That which does not have a two-finger-width mark is [not a bowl].
A "binding-place" bowl is one that has a two-finger-width mark.
"New" refers to a bowl that is so called by virtue of its being formally requested. "Should cause to be bartered for" means...
If she makes a request, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of proposing.
Upon receipt, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha.
Everyone must assemble having taken up their determined almsbowls.
One should not determine a low-quality bowl with the thought,
"I will take a valuable bowl."
If he resolves upon a wretched bowl with the thought, "I will take a costly bowl," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:

That monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak to them thus:
“Venerable sir, this bowl of mine was obtained by bartering for a bowl that had fewer than five mends;
it is to be relinquished. I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
Having relinquished it, the offense is to be confessed.
An offense should be accepted by a competent monk who is capable.
A monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the receiver of bowls:
one who would not fall into a wrong course through favoritism, nor through hatred, nor through delusion, nor through fear, and who would know what has been received and what has not been received.
“And furthermore, monks, it should be authorized in this way.
First, a monk should be requested.
Having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:”
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of alms-bowls.
This is the motion.
"Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs.
The Sangha appoints the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the distributor of alms-bowls.
Whosoever among the venerable ones approves of the appointment of the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the distributor of alms-bowls, let him be silent."
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of almsbowls.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent.
"I maintain this to be so.
Then the monk who has been appointed must bring forth the bowl.
The elder should be addressed as follows:
“Venerable sir, let the elder take the bowl.
If the elder takes it, the bowl must be given to the second person.
It must not be refused out of a lack of compassion. Whoever does not take it commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
It should not be given to one who has no bowl.
By this same method, it should be given down to the most junior member of the Saṅgha.
And whoever is the last person in that assembly of monks to have a bowl, he should be handed his bowl with these words: "Monk, you must keep this bowl until it breaks."
That monk must not set that bowl down in an improper place, nor use it for personal enjoyment, nor dispose of it, thinking, "How might this bowl be lost, destroyed, or broken?
If he sets it down in an improper place, uses it for personal enjoyment, or disposes of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This is the proper conduct in this matter.
This is the rule of conformity in this case.
If one exchanges an unbanded bowl for an unbanded bowl, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one exchanges an unbanded bowl for a bowl with a single band, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he exchanges a bowl with no repairs for a bowl with two repairs, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If he exchanges a bowl with no repairs for a bowl with three repairs, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If he exchanges a bowl with no repairs for a bowl with four repairs, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If he exchanges an alms-bowl with one repair for an alms-bowl with no repairs, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If he exchanges an alms-bowl with one repair for an alms-bowl with one repair, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If he exchanges an alms-bowl with one repair for an alms-bowl with two repairs, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one exchanges a bowl with a single band for a bowl with three bands, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If one exchanges a bowl with a single band for a bowl with four bands, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one exchanges a bowl with two bands for a bowl with no bands, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
With a bowl having two bands, [he exchanges] a bowl having one band … a bowl having two bands … a bowl having three bands … [and so on].

If he causes a bowl with four repairs to be exchanged for one with no repairs... [or] for one with three repairs... [or] for one with one repair, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If he causes a bowl with two bands, three bands,
or four bands to be made, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
A bowl with four repairs [exchanges for] a bowl without repairs ...
a bowl with one repair ...
a bowl with two repairs ... [and so forth].
If he causes an alms-bowl with three bands to be exchanged for one with four bands, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he causes an unbanded alms-bowl to be exchanged for an alms-bowl that has no place for bands, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
With a bowl that has no binding, one obtains a bowl with one binding; ... pe ...
a bowl with two binding places; ...
a bowl with three binding places.
If he causes an alms-bowl with four places for binding to be exchanged [for another], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
[Likewise] if he exchanges an alms-bowl with one place for binding for an alms-bowl without a place for binding ...
or an alms-bowl with one place for binding ... [it is an offense].
If he has a bowl with two binding points,
or a bowl with three binding points,
or a bowl with four binding points made up [from another], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If he causes a bowl with two binding places to be exchanged for a bowl with no binding places … [or] for a bowl with four binding places,

it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. If he causes a bowl with three binding places to be exchanged for a bowl with no binding places … [or] for a bowl with four binding places, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he causes an alms-bowl with four binding points to be exchanged for one with no binding points, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
[Likewise if he exchanges] an alms-bowl with four binding points for one with one binding point... [or] for one with no binding points... [or] for one with a single binding point... [etc.]
If he causes a bowl with two binding places to be exchanged,
or a bowl with three binding places to be exchanged,
or a bowl with four binding places to be exchanged, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If, with a bowl that has no binding, he exchanges it for a bowl that has no binding, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If, with a bowl that has no binding, he exchanges it for a bowl with one binding... [or] a bowl with two bindings... [it is likewise an offense of expiation involving forfeiture].
If he exchanges a bowl with three attachments for a bowl with four attachments, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If he exchanges a bowl with four attachments for a bowl with no attachments, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
With a bowl having four binding points, one may [exchange it for] a bowl with one binding point … a bowl with two binding points … a bowl with three binding points … [and so on].
If he causes a bowl with four binding points to be exchanged for one, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
[He exchanges] a bowl without a binding point for a bowl without a binding point …pe… a bowl with one binding point … [and so on].
If he causes a bowl with two places for binding to be exchanged,
or a bowl with three places for binding to be exchanged,
or a bowl with four places for binding to be exchanged, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
A bowl with four binding points [exchanging for] a bowl with no binding points …pe… a bowl with one binding point … a bowl with two binding points …
If he causes a bowl with three binding places to be exchanged for one with four binding places, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
There is no offense—
Of one whose bowl is lost,
of one whose bowl is broken,
[and] of relatives.
When [the monks] have been invited,
for the sake of another,
with one's own wealth.
"Of one who is insane,
of one who is a first-offender.
The second training rule on fewer than five stitches is concluded.
